claims.text: Controlled chromium microsegregation at critical microstructural sites improves corrosion resistance in carbon and low-alloy steels.
Chromium microsegregation enhances the formation and stability of a self-healing passive oxide film.
Carbon and low-alloy steels produced by standard casting exhibit a uniform chromium distribution.
Changing solidification cooling rates and subsequent heat treatments can induce targeted chromium segregation at grain boundaries and interdendritic regions.
Slow cooling promotes a relatively uniform chromium distribution.
Localized chromium enrichment at grain boundaries and interdendritic regions provides nucleation sites for a robust passive oxide film.
Chromium-induced local chemical gradients catalyze the nucleation and stabilization of passivating oxide films.
Chromium-enriched regions buffer the steel against chloride attack.
Chromium-enriched regions disrupt localized galvanic cells.
Chromium segregation promotes a more uniform and defect-reduced passive film.
Steels with controlled chromium segregation will exhibit lower corrosion current density than steels with uniform chromium distribution.
Steels with controlled chromium segregation will exhibit higher pitting potentials than steels with uniform chromium distribution.
The degree of chromium segregation will correlate positively with improved passive-film properties.
Conventional slow cooling followed by prolonged homogenization yields a uniform chromium distribution.
The proposed mechanism applies to carbon and low-alloy steels under chloride-containing electrolytes and processing conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
